n: Cathedral of the Resurrection and St. Thomas the Apostle, Zamość
w: Bernardo Morando, an Italian architect, modeled this late-16th-century church on the Renaissance churches of his homeland when Jan Zamoyski commissioned it as his new town's collegiate church. It sat on the Route of Renaissance for four centuries before Pope John Paul II raised it to cathedral rank in 1992.
_facts: Built late 16th century for city founder Jan Zamoyski
Designed by Italian architect Bernardo Morando
Was a collegiate church until 1992, when raised to cathedral status
Part of the Route of Renaissance

w: Completed in 1618 for the town's Polish Jewish congregation, this Renaissance synagogue survived the war only because the Nazis gutted its interior into a carpenters' workshop rather than destroying it outright. Restored from 2005, it now runs as a Jewish museum within the UNESCO-listed Old City of Zamosc.
s: 1618 synagogue, saved by becoming a workshop
_facts: Completed in 1618 in the Renaissance style
Interior turned into a carpenters' workshop by Nazi occupiers in WWII
UNESCO World Heritage Site, part of the Old City of Zamość
Restored from 2005, now operates as a Jewish museum

w: Officially the Church of the Annunciation, but everyone calls it the Franciscan Church - at 56 metres long and 29 wide, it is the largest church in town and was ranked among Poland's most prominent 17th-century Baroque buildings. It still anchors the skyline of the Old Town today.
s: Zamosc's biggest church, Baroque and blunt
_facts: Baroque Franciscan church, dedicated to the Annunciation
56 metres long, 29 metres wide - largest church in Zamość
Regarded as one of Poland's most prominent 17th-century churches

w: Jan Zamoyski began fortifying his new city in 1579, and the result held off Cossacks, Swedes and Russians through six sieges over two and a half centuries - including an eight-month siege in 1813 that ended only when the Polish garrison surrendered. Demolished in 1866 once obsolete, only fragments survive today.
_facts: Built 1579-1618 by Chancellor Jan Zamoyski
Withstood six sieges including Cossacks, Swedes and Russians
The 1813 siege lasted 8 months before Polish garrison surrendered
Demolished in 1866; only fragments remain

w: A former Nazi German Gestapo camp on the edge of town, used during the German AB-Aktion and the ethnic cleansing of the surrounding region in WWII. It is now the Museum of Martyrdom of the Zamosc Region, a stark memorial to the atrocities carried out here on occupied Polish soil.
s: Former Gestapo camp, now a WWII memorial
_facts: Former Nazi German Gestapo camp near Zamość
Tied to the AB-Aktion and ethnic cleansing of the Zamość region
Now the Museum of Martyrdom of the Zamość Region

w: Founded in 1926, this museum fills the upper floors of restored Renaissance tenement houses built by Armenian immigrants who settled here from 1585 under privileges granted by Jan Zamoyski. Six departments - archaeology, ethnography, general history, the Rotunda, a library and education - trace the city's layered past.
_facts: Founded 1926, located in the Old City UNESCO site
Housed in Renaissance tenements built by Armenian settlers from 1585
Six departments: archaeology, library, ethnography, general history, the Rotunda, education

n: Sacred Museum of the Zamość Cathedral
w: Opened in 1987 in a former prelate's house by the cathedral, this museum guards the coronation alb of King Michal Korybut Wisniowiecki alongside 16th- and 17th-century vestments, reliquaries and coffin portraits of past prelates. A 2018-19 restoration split it across two buildings, the Infulatka and the Vicarage.
s: Cathedral treasury: a king's coronation alb
_facts: Opened March 1987 at the Zamość Cathedral prelate building
Holds the coronation alb of King Michal Korybut Wisniowiecki
Collection includes 16th-17th century vestments, reliquaries and coffin portraits
Since 2020, split across the Infulatka and Vicarage buildings after 2018-19 restoration
